summary: RFC 8784 lets IKEv2 use a pre-shared post-quantum key so IPsec traffic stays safe from later decryption by a quantum computer. This document describes how to mix such preshared keys in the IKE_INTERMEDIATE and CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges to strengthen post-quantum protection.

eli5.summary: Even if someone records secret messages now, a future super-computer should not be able to read them. This adds an extra secret shared in advance to make that harder.

questions: how does ikev2 use a post-quantum preshared key
how is rfc 9867 different from rfc 8784
subtitle: Mixing a post-quantum preshared key into IKEv2 earlier, so even the initial IKE SA is protected, and again later when rekeying.

tldr.problem: RFC 8784 mixes a Post-quantum Preshared Key (PPK) into IKEv2 only in the IKE_AUTH exchange, leaving the initial IKE SA unprotected and offering no way to use a fresh PPK without deleting the IKE SA.
tldr.mechanism: The peers negotiate a new USE_PPK_INT notification, exchange PPK identities in the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange and recompute the IKE SA keys from the PPK. They can also mix a fresh PPK into SK_d in CREATE_CHILD_SA.
tldr.outcome: The initial IKE SA and the IKE_AUTH exchange become quantum secure, at the cost of an extra round trip unless IKE_INTERMEDIATE is used anyway. It complements RFC 8784 and does not replace it.

today: RFC 9867 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it works alongside RFC 8784 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: Why RFC 8784 Was Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 8784 lets IKEv2 mix a Post-quantum Preshared Key (PPK) into the session key calculation, so IPsec traffic recorded today cannot be decrypted later by a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC). It protects the IPsec traffic but not the initial IKE SA, because extending protection there was thought to need serious changes to core IKEv2.

This leaves two gaps. First, some uses need the initial IKE SA protected from the start. The RFC's example is Group Key Management using IKEv2 (RFC 9838), where group policy and other sensitive data flow over the initial IKE SA. Second, RFC 8784 treats PPKs as static and uses them only once, so a fresh PPK, for example from Quantum Key Distribution, could be used only by deleting the IKE SA and starting over.

This document fixes both by using the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange (RFC 9242) and the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange. It does not replace RFC 8784.
sections.eli5: The old trick protected the secret packages but not the first chat, and you could not swap in a fresh shared secret later. This adds both.

sections.title: Negotiating a PPK for the Initial IKE SA
sections.content:
An initiator that supports IKE_INTERMEDIATE and wants a PPK includes the INTERMEDIATE_EXCHANGE_SUPPORTED and USE_PPK_INT notifications in the IKE_SA_INIT request. A responder that agrees returns both in its response. USE_PPK_INT is a Status Type notification with Notify Message Type 16445, no SPI and empty data. Implementations MUST ignore any data in it they do not understand.

This negotiation is independent of RFC 8784. An initiator may offer both USE_PPK_INT and USE_PPK, but the responder MUST return only one of them. If the initiator did not propose this extension and the responder's policy requires a PPK on the initial IKE SA, the responder MUST return NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN.
sections.eli5: First the two sides just say 'I know the secret handshake, do you?' If both do, they continue.

sections.title: Proposing and Choosing a PPK
sections.content:
After a successful negotiation, the initiator sends one or more PPK_IDENTITY_KEY notifications in the IKE_INTERMEDIATE request. If several IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges happen, they go in the last one before IKE_AUTH. This is a Status Type notification with Notify Message Type 16446. Its data holds a PPK_ID as defined in RFC 8784, followed by an 8-octet PPK Confirmation.

The confirmation is the first 8 octets of prf( PPK, Ni | Nr | SPIi | SPIr ). It lets the responder check that it holds the same PPK for that ID without revealing the key.

The responder then has three outcomes. If it has a matching PPK, it replies with a PPK_IDENTITY notification naming it, and the initiator MUST abort if that ID was never proposed. If it has no match and PPK use is mandatory, it MUST return AUTHENTICATION_FAILED. If it has no match and use is optional, it sends no PPK identity, and the initiator MUST abort if quantum resistance is a requirement.
sections.eli5: The first side lists the handshakes it knows plus a quick proof it really knows each one. The other side picks one it also knows, or says no.

sections.title: What the Responder Does
sections.content:
The responder's behavior follows from three questions: did the initiator propose this extension, does the responder hold one of the proposed PPKs with a matching value, and is a PPK mandatory for the initial IKE SA. If nothing was proposed and a PPK is not mandatory, it falls back to RFC 8784 if that was proposed, or to standard IKEv2.

The responder picks a PPK before it knows who the initiator is. In IKE_AUTH it may therefore find that the chosen PPK is not allowed for that identity under its local policy. It SHOULD then abort and return AUTHENTICATION_FAILED, but MAY continue with the negotiated PPK if its local policy accepts that.
sections.eli5: The picker chooses before it knows exactly who is asking. If it later finds the choice was not allowed for that person, it normally stops.

sections.title: Computing the Keys
sections.content:
Once a PPK is agreed in IKE_INTERMEDIATE, the IKE SA keys are recalculated. If other actions in the same exchange also recompute keys (for example RFC 9370), applying the PPK MUST come last, just before the keys are used in the next exchange.

A new SKEYSEED' is computed as prf+ (PPK, SK_d) from the PPK and the most recent SK_d, exactly as RFC 8784 applies a PPK to SK_d. All the SK_* keys are then derived from SKEYSEED', Ni, Nr, SPIi and SPIr following Section 2.14 of RFC 7296. Unlike in RFC 8784, SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr are not separately recalculated with the PPK afterwards.

For CREATE_CHILD_SA the mixing is simpler: SK_d' = prf+ (PPK, SK_d), and SK_d' replaces SK_d in the usual formulas for the new SA.
sections.eli5: The shared secret is stirred into the key recipe before any important messages are sent, so a thief who records them still cannot make the keys.

sections.title: Fresh PPKs in CREATE_CHILD_SA
sections.content:
If both peers get a fresh PPK while an IKE SA is active, they MAY use it when creating additional IPsec SAs or rekeying IKE or IPsec SAs. This works whether or not the current IKE SA was created with a PPK, by any method.

The initiator adds one or more PPK_IDENTITY_KEY notifications to the CREATE_CHILD_SA request. Here the PPK Confirmation is the first 8 octets of prf( PPK, Ni | SPIi | SPIr ), where Ni is the nonce in that request and the SPIs belong to the current IKE SA. A willing responder answers with a PPK_IDENTITY notification naming its choice.

Without a match or support, the responder includes no PPK_IDENTITY and the new SA is made as in plain IKEv2. The initiator can delete that SA if it is unacceptable. If PPK use is mandatory for the responder in this exchange and no usable PPK was offered, it MUST return NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN. If the PPK has not changed since the IKE SA was set up, using it again gains nothing.
sections.eli5: Whenever the two sides get a brand-new shared secret, they can start using it for new locked boxes right away, without hanging up and starting the whole call again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General security considerations for PPKs in IKEv2 are in RFC 8784. This specification makes even the initial IKE SA quantum secure. A PPK is mixed into the SK_* keys before IKE_AUTH starts, and since the PPK is also used in authentication, the exchange is quantum secure even against an active attacker.

It relies on IKE_INTERMEDIATE, so the security issues in RFC 9242 apply. The document also repeats that symmetric-key primitives are believed not to be affected by a CRQC, as discussed in Section 4 of RFC 9370.
sections.eli5: Because the shared secret goes in before the sensitive messages, even someone who can tamper with the conversation cannot use a quantum computer to break in.

sections.title: Comparison with RFC 8784
sections.content:
The document stresses that it is not a replacement for PPKs in IKE_AUTH. Use it when that approach does not meet requirements, such as a quantum-secure initial IKE SA or a choice among several PPKs. Peers supporting both may use this one even where IKE_AUTH would suffice.

Advantages: IKE_AUTH, including ID payloads, is fully protected. The initial IKE SA is protected too, which matters when it carries sensitive data such as CREATE_CHILD_SA traffic or the G-IKEv2 GSA_REGISTRATION exchange. The initiator can propose several PPKs and the responder picks one, which could simplify PPK rollover. And the initiator need not compute the AUTH payload twice when PPK use is optional for both sides.

The main disadvantage is an additional round trip, the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange. If that exchange is needed for other purposes anyway, the PPK payloads can be piggybacked on it and the penalty disappears.
sections.eli5: The new way is safer from the very first message and lets you pick among secrets, but costs one more back-and-forth unless that trip was happening anyway.
